Ilbenstadt
IL-bun-shtat
n. (the Wetterau Premonstratensian abbey of 1123, endowed by Gottfried of Cappenberg)
From a Germanic personal name with Stadt, a place or settlement.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ilbenstadt in the Wetterau north of Frankfurt was founded in 1123 and given to Norbert's new order, and its Romanesque basilica of about 1159 survives nearly intact. Its endowment came from Gottfried, count of Cappenberg in Westphalia, who in 1122 handed Norbert his ancestral castle and his entire inheritance to be made into monasteries, over the furious objection of his father-in-law, and who entered the order himself and died at twenty-six. His brother Otto followed him. Ilbenstadt holds the graves of both. This dictionary records Ilbenstadt because Gottfried did what the rich young ruler would not, and the comparison is worth making carefully. The command was given to one man whose possessions held him, “go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mar 10:21), and the refusal is one of the saddest lines in the Gospels, “he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22). Christ says plainly where a heart will be found, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mat 6:21), and he names the choice as a choice between masters, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor; to renounce as to disown or reject; patrimony as an estate inherited from one's father; endowment as a permanent provision; and mammon as riches, wealth personified.

expand to see more

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; an estate which a man has by descent, as the heir to another.

RENOUNCE, v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; to cast off; to forsake; as, to renounce a claim or a title.

PATRIMONY, n. A right or estate inherited from one's ancestors; particularly, from a father; a church estate or revenue.

ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution; the fund so settled.

MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth; or the god of riches; a word used by our Saviour as the personification of worldly gain.

Key Scripture

Mar 10:21 — "Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me."

Mat 19:22 — "But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions."

Mat 6:21 — "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Modern Corruption

Wetterau abbey of 1123, endowed by a count who gave Norbert his castle and his whole inheritance and died a canon at twenty-six.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the diagnostic. The command to sell was given to a particular man because his possessions had him, and Christ's general rule explains why he could put it that way, “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mat 6:21). Gottfried of Cappenberg handed over castles his family had held for generations, and his relatives reacted exactly as one would expect.

The caution is against reading this as a universal rule or a merit. Scripture does not command every believer to divest, and it never treats poverty as purchase. What it does is force a choice of master, in terms that allow no arrangement, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). The rich young man heard the same words and left, and the text gives his reason without comment, “for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22). The question is not how much a man has but which way he walks when told to let go.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek poleo (G4453), to sell; Greek ktema (G2933), a possession; Greek thesauros (G2344), treasure; Greek mamonas (G3126), mammon; Greek lupeo (G3076), to grieve.

expand to see more

Greek poleo (G4453) — to sell, said to one man; “sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor”, Mark 10:21.

Greek ktema (G2933) — a possession, here many; “for he had great possessions”, Matthew 19:22.

Greek lupeo (G3076) — to be grieved, to go away sorrowful; “he went away sorrowful”, Matthew 19:22.

Greek thesauros (G2344) — treasure, and the heart follows it; “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also”, Matthew 6:21.

Greek mamonas (G3126) — mammon, wealth personified as a master; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”, Matthew 6:24.

Usage

"“sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mar 10:21) — what a count of Cappenberg actually did."

"“he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22) — the other man, given the same word."

"“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24) — the choice that allows no arrangement."
